episode.title: Cariboo Signals - Working Lands & Industry
episode.description:
Riley and Casey explore technology and society in rural communities. Today's focus: Working Lands & Industry.

THIS WEEK WE'RE ASKING: Does a place still exist if nobody records it?

NEWS ROUNDUP: We break down [Williams Lake Tribune] Quesnel man whose life ‘was off the rails’ spending another 88 days in jail and [My Cariboo Now] Man sentenced in connection with serious incident outside a temporary shelter in Quesnel, plus 1 more stories, and explore what these developments mean for communities like ours.

RURAL CONNECTIONS: When working lands are managed using satellite data and remote sensors, how do communities ensure that ground-truth knowledge from experienced workers like cruisers and ranchers has standing in tenure and management decisions? Topics include: The role of satellite imagery and LiDAR in forestry management versus local expertise, Mill curtailments and the loss of experienced cruisers and fallers as institutional knowledge, Data gaps in timber flow tracking and the Red Rock weigh station example, Range health assessments on Crown grazing tenure versus daily rancher observations, Existing models like community forest reporting and potential mechanisms like tenure conditions or liaison committees.

Hosts: Riley (Tech optimist with an engineering background) and Casey (Community-first skeptic of tech promises).

COMMUNITY SPOTLIGHT: Cariboo Chilcotin Coast Tourism Association

discussion.central_question: When working lands are managed using satellite data and remote sensors, how do communities ensure that ground-truth knowledge from experienced workers like cruisers and ranchers has standing in tenure and management decisions?
discussion.riley_position: Satellite imagery and LiDAR provide detailed canopy data, but they cannot capture crucial ground-level knowledge about drainage conditions, soil stability, and real-time land changes that only experienced workers walking the land actually know.
riley_key_evidence: LiDAR flights from 400 kilometres up give canopy height and stand density but miss specific problems like root rot or unstable ground after burns
When mills curtail and lay off their highest-paid, most experienced cruisers first, the region loses the only people who knew what was actually standing beyond what sensors register
Weigh station records exist but don't feed into public dashboards that communities could use to check against mill curtailment numbers
discussion.casey_position: The infrastructure to track working land data exists (weigh stations, range assessments, harvest records), but communities and local knowledge-holders are excluded from formal decision-making processes, and no structural mechanism exists to reconcile local observations with official provincial records.
casey_key_evidence: Ranchers standing on their land every day could report range degradation within a season, but when province-conducted range assessments arrive years apart, there's no formal channel to reconcile disagreements and the province's record wins by default
Tenure decisions are made only by province, licensee, and hired consultants—never by the town whose mill curtailed 100 jobs
Some community forests already publish harvest and silviculture data publicly, but this model hasn't spread across licensee-held tenure covering most of the Cariboo's working forest
discussion.resolution: Neither party conceded their position. Instead, they identified a regulatory gap rather than a technology gap: the Forest Act doesn't require ground-truth reconciliation with local knowledge, and tenure renewal cycles run on decade-long timescales, meaning structural fixes arrive too slowly to help workers already laid off. They agreed that several tools exist on paper but require political will to implement.
topics_covered: The role of satellite imagery and LiDAR in forestry management versus local expertise
Mill curtailments and the loss of experienced cruisers and fallers as institutional knowledge
Data gaps in timber flow tracking and the Red Rock weigh station example
Range health assessments on Crown grazing tenure versus daily rancher observations
Existing models like community forest reporting and potential mechanisms like tenure conditions or liaison committees
calls_to_action: A community forest board or producer association could keep its own running log of harvest volumes, range conditions, and mill throughput to cross-check against provincial data, following the precedent of watershed groups tracking stream flow independently

Make local reporting a condition of tenure holding, tied to the permit itself rather than to corporate ownership, similar to Impact Benefit Agreements, so obligations survive corporate sales and curtailments

A town could establish a local forest liaison committee made up of retired fallers and cruisers meeting a couple times a year to compare notes against the licensee's latest cut plan—requiring only a room and licensee willingness, not legislative change

If you've sat through a tenure review hearing or serve on a community forest board, share what working reconciliation between local knowledge and official records actually looks like by sending feedback to cariboo signals dot c-a
